A Short Field Guide to Lighthouses

This guide was written for the tests of a small program. It
describes an imaginary lighthouse and the people who look
after it. Nothing in it is meant as advice for real keepers, and
every name in it is invented.
The introduction is short on purpose. It stands before the first
heading, so a careful reader of the file should treat it as a part
of its own.

Chapter 1: The Lamp Room
The lamp room sits at the top of ninety-two steps. Every
evening the keeper climbs them with a can of oil, a clean cloth
and a well-thumbed note-book. The glass is wiped first, because salt gathers on it during the day and a dull lens throws
a dull beam.
When the wick is trimmed the keeper lights it and waits. The
flame needs a quarter of an hour to settle, and nobody hurries
it. Only then is the great lens set turning, slowly, on its bed of
rollers.
On clear nights the beam can be seen from the far side of the
bay. Fishing crews say that it looks like a patient hand, waving
them home.
